analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from forcing workers and consumers to sign away their right to sue before a dispute happens.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 81 House members, never received a hearing or a vote and died in the House Judiciary Committee when the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies increasingly require employees and customers to agree in advance to settle any dispute in private arbitration instead of court, using clauses buried in job paperwork and consumer contracts. This bill would make those pre-dispute arbitration clauses unenforceable for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights cases, and would give courts — not arbitrators — the power to decide whether an arbitration agreement is valid. People could still choose arbitration after a dispute arises, and union contracts would keep their existing arbitration systems.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees with discrimination or wage claims, consumers with disputes involving credit, purchases, or investments, and people injured by antitrust violations — anyone who today is routed into private arbitration they agreed to without real bargaining. It also preserves class action lawsuits, which are typically the only practical way to challenge small-dollar harms like illegal fees.

how_it_helps.text: Declares that no pre-dispute arbitration agreement is valid or enforceable if it covers an employment, consumer, antitrust, or civil rights dispute.
Gives courts, rather than arbitrators, the power to decide whether an arbitration agreement is valid and enforceable, no matter how the challenge to it is framed.

Keeps voluntary, post-dispute arbitration available, and leaves arbitration in collective bargaining agreements in place — while ensuring those union agreements cannot waive an employee's right to enforce constitutional or statutory rights in court.

analysis.who_pays: Large employers, banks, credit card issuers, securities and investment firms, and other businesses that rely on mandatory arbitration clauses to resolve disputes outside of court, where cases are private, cheaper for the company, harder to appeal, and cannot be combined into class actions. Arbitration providers would also lose the high volume of forced consumer and employment cases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large employers and consumer finance firms

drawbacks.text: Businesses argue that arbitration is faster and cheaper for everyone, and that ending mandatory arbitration pushes more cases into slow, costly court litigation.

Some individual claims are small enough that a court case costs more than the recovery, so without class actions the dispute may simply never be brought — a risk the bill does not address beyond preserving class actions generally.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are substantial and concrete: restoring the right to a day in court for discrimination, wage, consumer, and civil rights claims that millions of people currently sign away without realizing it. The costs fall mainly on companies that prefer a private, company-friendly dispute system, plus the genuine risk that some small claims go unpursued — but the bill keeps voluntary arbitration and class actions available, which is the standard remedy for small-dollar harms.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee — specifically in a subcommittee on regulatory reform and antitrust — from June 2013 until the Congress ended in January 2015, without a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Hank Johnson introduced the bill on May 7, 2013 with 22 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
On June 14, 2013 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law, where it remained for the rest of the Congress.
The bill attracted 81 cosponsors, all Democrats, but was never reported out of committee and never received a vote in the House before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large employers and consumer-facing finance companies are better off: mandatory arbitration clauses remain enforceable, so disputes over discrimination, wages, fees, and debt continue to be resolved in private arbitration instead of court. Arbitration providers also keep the case volume these clauses generate.

for.name: Rep. Hank Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 22 original cosponsors on introduction day.

for.name: 81 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 81 were Democrats.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee on June 14, 2013 and never brought it to a hearing, a committee markup, or the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 81 cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-led Judiciary Committee never moved the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

industries.note: Mandatory arbitration clauses let employers resolve wage, discrimination, and civil rights claims privately, without juries, class actions, or meaningful appeal. The bill would have taken that shield away, so its interest runs against the employees seeking those remedies.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and investment firms
industries.note: Consumer finance contracts routinely force fee, debt, and securities disputes into arbitration. The bill's definition of consumer disputes explicitly covers securities and investment services, and it would have preserved class actions — the main tool for challenging small-dollar illegal fees.

Private arbitration firms earn fees from the huge volume of forced consumer and employment cases. Invalidating pre-dispute agreements would eliminate most of that business, leaving only voluntary post-dispute arbitration.
The bill expressly preserves arbitration in union contracts, while ensuring those agreements cannot waive an employee's right to enforce constitutional and statutory rights in court.
